title: Feedback-Enhanced Quantum Metrology And Clock Precision Under Thermodynamic Uncertainty
authors: Chen Wang Jincheng Lu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.00622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Feedback can convert continuously monitored quantum jumps into a thermodynamic resource. We formulate full counting statistics for open quantum systems under unital jump feedback by incorporating the feedback maps into the tilted generator. The resulting trajectory ensemble determines both current fluctuations and the Fisher information of the measurement record. We show that feedback can enhance reservoir-parameter estimation and clock precision without necessarily changing average thermodynamic currents. This enhanced precision is not bounded by reservoir entropy production alone. By embedding the reduced dynamics in an enlarged measurement-feedback process, we derive a feedback-modified thermodynamic uncertainty relation in which the information entropy production of the feedback apparatus supplies the missing cost. A charge-monitored double quantum dot illustrates the framework: jump-conditioned feedback improves thermometry and chemical-potential sensing, and stabilizes a quantum clock defined by output-current ticks.
tldr: The paper develops a full counting statistics framework for open quantum systems with feedback, showing that feedback can enhance measurement precision and clock stability without necessarily increasing average thermodynamic currents, and derives a feedback-modified thermodynamic uncertainty relation.
motivation: To understand how feedback, a potential thermodynamic resource, affects the precision of quantum metrology and clocks, and to characterize the thermodynamic cost via modified uncertainty relations.
method: They incorporate feedback into the tilted generator to formulate full counting statistics, and derive a feedback-modified thermodynamic uncertainty relation by embedding the reduced dynamics in an enlarged measurement-feedback process.
result: They show that feedback can enhance parameter estimation and clock precision without altering average currents, and that the cost is captured by the information entropy production of the feedback apparatus. A double quantum dot example illustrates improvements in thermometry and chemical potential sensing.
conclusion: Feedback provides a way to surpass standard thermodynamic uncertainty bounds, with the missing cost supplied by information entropy production, offering new insights for quantum metrology and clock design.

title: Strengthened Second Law For Periodic Processes
authors: Jake Schaefer, Ben Ansbacher, Jan Korbel, David H. Wolpert
abstract: ArXiv:2609.00639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many physical systems evolve under periodic driving: the same control protocol is applied again and again, even though the state of the system itself need not return to where it started after each cycle. We derive a physics-independent lower bound on the entropy production of periodic process modeled by the evolution of an initial distribution [MATH] by a repeated application of the same map [MATH]. This is a strict strengthening of the second law of thermodynamics for periodic processes. It does not require that the single-period dynamics arise from a CTMC, satisfy (local) detailed balance, or be subject to other typical restrictions. We discuss its application to spins in the Curie-Weiss model and Deterministic Finite Automata, with possible extensions to other uniform computers.
tldr: Derives a physics-independent lower bound on entropy production for periodically driven processes, strictly strengthening the second law without requiring typical restrictions like CTMC or detailed balance.
motivation: To understand thermodynamic constraints on systems under periodic driving, where the state does not need to return to its initial condition, and to provide a more robust second law applicable to a wider class of processes.
method: Uses an information-theoretic approach, modeling the evolution of an initial distribution by repeated application of a map, and derives a general inequality for entropy production that holds for any periodic process.
result: A strict strengthening of the second law for periodic processes, with applications demonstrated in the Curie-Weiss model and Deterministic Finite Automata, suggesting broader implications for uniform computers.
conclusion: Provides a fundamental thermodynamic bound that is independent of specific physical mechanisms, enhancing our understanding of nonequilibrium thermodynamics and its information-processing counterparts.

The bound is derived from the contraction of relative entropy (or Kullback-Leibler divergence) under the map, and it strictly strengthens the second law of thermodynamics for such processes. Notably, the result does not require the dynamics to be Markovian at the level of a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC), nor does it require detailed balance or other typical physical constraints, making it applicable to a wide range of systems, including computational processes. The authors illustrate the bound on two examples: spins in the Curie-Weiss model and Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA), and suggest extensions to other uniform computers.

For periodic processes, they take the limit N→∞ and obtain a lower bound that is strictly positive if the initial distribution is not stationary. The proof is general and does not rely on specific physical assumptions, making the result robust and widely applicable. title: Alternative-mean Trace Divergences: Geometry, Data Processing, And Barycenters
authors: Trung Dung Vuong, Hiroki Shudo, Hiroyuki Osaka
abstract: ArXiv:2609.00034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a nontrivial normalized operator monotone function and set [MATH]. We introduce the alternative-mean trace functional $[MATH][MATH]\altPhi_f[MATH][MATH]$.
tldr: Introduces alternative-mean trace divergences based on operator monotone functions and studies their geometric and information-theoretic properties.
motivation: To generalize existing quantum divergences and provide new measures with desirable properties like data processing.
method: Uses operator monotone functions to define alternative-mean trace functionals, and analyzes their mathematical structure.
result: Establishes data processing inequalities, geometric interpretations, and existence/uniqueness of barycenters.
conclusion: Offers new tools for quantifying quantum state distinguishability and potentially for quantum protocols.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a new trace functional, termed the alternative-mean trace functional, defined for positive definite matrices A and B using an operator monotone function f. This functional, denoted altPhi_f(A,B), is constructed as the difference between the trace of the weighted arithmetic mean (with weight s = f'(1)) and a correction term involving the geometric mean and f. The main result proves that altPhi_f is a quantum divergence in the sense of Bhatia-Gaubert-Jain, meaning it satisfies certain positivity and metric properties. Specifically, its diagonal Hessian induces a positive multiple of the Bures-Wasserstein Riemannian metric. The paper also establishes sharp two-sided inequalities relating altPhi_f to the squared Bures-Wasserstein distance, with constants s(1-s) and (1-s+s^2). These results generalize and refine known inequalities for quantum divergences, providing a new family of divergences parameterized by operator monotone functions.

Proves that altPhi_f is a quantum divergence in the sense of Bhatia-Gaubert-Jain, with its diagonal Hessian yielding a positive multiple of the Bures-Wasserstein metric.

Provides a unified framework that recovers known results for specific choices of f (e.g., f(t)=t and f(t)=log t) and offers new insights into the geometry of quantum state spaces.

The authors define the alternative-mean trace functional using the Kubo-Ando operator means, specifically the weighted arithmetic mean and the geometric mean. The proof of the quantum divergence property relies on establishing the joint convexity and other inequalities for the functional, likely using techniques from operator monotone functions and trace inequalities. The proportionality constant is shown to be positive, specifically a multiple of s(1-s), which is positive for nontrivial f. The results are significant as they offer a new class of divergences with metric properties, potentially useful in quantum information theory and quantum state estimation.

title: Entangling Capability Of Coherently Controlled Quantum Processes
authors: Beyza Aslanba\c{s}, Bedirhan Alkan, G\"oktu\u{g} Karpat
abstract: ArXiv:2609.00168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analytically characterize entanglement generation by two paradigmatic coherently controlled quantum processes, the quantum switch and time-flip. Retaining rather than measuring or discarding the control, we treat the control and target as the bipartite system and assume pure product inputs, so that any output entanglement reflects the entangling capability of the process. For the switch of qubit unitaries, we derive exact expressions for entanglement, together with a geometric characterization and a coherence-entanglement conservation relation. We then extend our analysis to binary random unitary, Pauli, amplitude damping, and generalized amplitude damping channels. We prove that switch of channels commuting under composition cannot entangle a separable input. Yet maximal entanglement is possible even with dissipation, e.g., an entanglement-breaking damping channel switched with a bit-flip can transform a product input into a maximally entangled state. For two generalized amplitude damping channels, a common stationary state prevents entanglement, while different stationary populations can enable it. We present an analogous study for the time-flip of unitary and binary random unitary channels. Our findings provide a systematic analysis of how much entanglement can be generated by coherent control of channel order or input-output direction.
tldr: This paper analytically characterizes the entangling capability of coherently controlled quantum processes (quantum switch and time-flip) by deriving exact entanglement expressions and conservation relations.
motivation: Understanding how coherent control of quantum processes affects entanglement generation is fundamental for quantum information processing, as entanglement is a key resource.
method: Treating control and target as a bipartite system with pure product inputs, the authors derive exact entanglement formulas for various channels, including qubit unitaries and damping channels, and prove conditions for entanglement generation.
result: They find that switch of commuting channels cannot entangle, yet maximal entanglement is possible even with dissipative channels when suitably controlled, and they provide analogous results for time-flip.
conclusion: The work offers a systematic analysis of how coherent control of channel order or input-output direction can serve as a resource for entanglement generation.

title: Quantum Secret Sharing With A Helper And Programmable Access Structures
authors: Eric Chitambar, Sarah Hagen, David W. Kribs, Mike I. Nelson, Andrew Nemec
abstract: ArXiv:2609.00220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum secret sharing (QSS) is a process in which the state of a quantum system is partitioned into multiple shares, allowing only specific subsets of shareholders to reconstruct the state, while others gain no information about its identity. In this work, we propose a variant of QSS, called ``helper QSS,'' which designates a special shareholder whose participation with any other group of parties is sufficient for recovering the state. We present different families of helper codes that function for an arbitrary number of parties and system sizes. As an application, we introduce the idea of a programmable access structure in QSS, which allows for a third-party programmer to independently choose the access structure of the code even after the shares are delivered to all the shareholders. This choice is made blindly, meaning that the programmer has no information about the secret being encoded, and it is implemented using the nonlocal process of quantum steering.
tldr: This paper introduces helper quantum secret sharing (QSS), where a special helper enables recovery with any other party, and presents programmable access structures using quantum steering.
motivation: Traditional QSS requires specific subsets to reconstruct the secret; this work aims to add flexibility by designating a helper and allowing programmable access structures without knowing the secret.
method: The authors propose helper QSS schemes and construct families of codes for arbitrary parties and system sizes. They also demonstrate programmable access structures using quantum steering, allowing a third party to choose the access structure after share distribution.
result: They present various helper code families and show how the programmable access structure can be implemented via nonlocal steering.
conclusion: The work extends QSS capabilities, enabling more flexible and dynamic secret sharing with potential applications in quantum networks.

title: Which Otto Engine Is The Fastest?
authors: Marcin {\l}obejko Idriss Hank Nkouatchoua Ngueya
abstract: ArXiv:2609.00321v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A general thermal machine is characterized by distinct time or energy scales: temperature, coupling to the heat baths, internal free dynamics and interactions, and external driving. We address the question: what parameters determine the speed of a given engine, and how can they be used to reliably compare different types of engine? Specifically, we consider four realizations of the Otto engine, each operating with the same Otto efficiency, and aim to characterize and compare their power outputs. The main insight of this paper is that, irrespective of their very different dynamical implementations, the power of each engine can be factorized into a common characteristic work and an implementation-specific characteristic time. The characteristic work depends only on the internal frequencies of the machine and the temperatures, whereas the characteristic time depends on the coupling strength to the baths and on the implementation-specific driving. This observation allows us to compare the power of different engines through their characteristic times and thereby reduce the relevant parameter space to parameters that capture the dynamical aspects of engine performance. Despite different dynamical implementations, this framework reveals simple common features. In all cases, the maximum operating speed is limited by a common timescale given by the sum of the characteristic thermalization times of the hot and cold baths. Moreover, the four engines fall into two distinct asymptotic classes: implementations in which driving and thermalization occur simultaneously exhibit quadratic scaling, whereas those in which work extraction and thermalization alternate exhibit linear scaling. These results expose general dynamical features that determine the operational speed of quantum Otto engines.
tldr: This paper introduces a framework to compare the power of different quantum Otto engines by factoring performance into a characteristic work and an implementation-specific characteristic time, revealing common scaling laws.
motivation: To understand what determines the speed of quantum thermal machines and enable reliable comparison between different engine designs.
method: The authors analyze four different realizations of the Otto engine with the same efficiency, derive characteristic time and work, and study their scaling with parameters.
result: They find that the maximum speed is limited by the sum of thermalization times of hot and cold baths, and identify two asymptotic classes with linear or quadratic scaling depending on whether driving and thermalization overlap.
conclusion: The framework reduces the parameter space and exposes universal dynamical constraints on engine speed, providing a basis for optimizing quantum Otto engines.

title: Codes For Quantum Secret Sharing With A Helper
authors: Eric Chitambar, Sarah Hagen, David W. Kribs, Zhao Ma, Mike I. Nelson, Andrew Nemec
abstract: ArXiv:2609.00234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Helper quantum secret sharing is a form of secret sharing defined by its unique access structure. One special fixed party, called the helper, can work together with any other party to fully decode the secret. A blind helper is one who can provide this assistance while not holding any local information about the encoded secret. In this work, we analyze the general structure of QSS helper codes and present new code constructions. We fully characterize the structure of blind helper stabilizer codes and show that for the encoding of a single qubit, recovery is always possible using one-way local operations and classical communication (LOCC) from the helper to the targeted party. Furthermore, we demonstrate how such codes also allow for the helper to target larger subsets of parties by one-way LOCC, enabling them to be authorized to recover the secret. Finally, when each party only holds a qubit, we identify the general form of all helper codes (including non-stabilizer codes) and find that LOCC recovery is only possible in special cases.

title: Exact Learning Of Quantum Noise With Tensor Networks
authors: Nicola Pancotti, Vedika Saravanan, Krysta Svore
abstract: ArXiv:2609.00169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate noise models are essential for high-performance quantum error correction, yet characterizing the noise of a quantum device typically requires dedicated experiments. We present a variational framework that learns the noise model directly from quantum-error-correction syndrome and logical-observable data collected during error-corrected memory experiments. The fault-event probabilities are treated as variational parameters and optimized via gradient descent to minimize the binary cross-entropy between the decoder's predictions and experimental logical-observable outcomes. We prove that this objective is principled rather than ad hoc: a sufficiently expressive noise ansatz attains the information-theoretic minimum logical error rate. We instantiate this framework using a tensor-network decoder, which provides exact maximum-likelihood decoding and analytically differentiable gradients with respect to all noise parameters. Using circuit-level data from Google's Sycamore processor, and starting from an uninformed prior, the optimization recovers noise models whose logical error rates agree to within [MATH] with those of Google's independently characterized detector error model. The mean squared error between the learned and reference noise parameters shows a clear overall decrease throughout training, confirming that the method recovers physically meaningful noise structure, not merely parameters that happen to decode well. We further demonstrate that the optimization can track device drifts in real time via warm-started updates, maintaining near-optimal decoding performance under synthetically evolving noise without the need for re-characterization. The approach is decoder-agnostic in its formulation and naturally extends to correlated noise models.
tldr: A variational framework using tensor-network decoders learns quantum noise models directly from error-corrected memory data, achieving near-optimal logical error rates and tracking device drifts.
motivation: Accurate noise models are critical for quantum error correction, but conventional characterization requires dedicated experiments; learning noise from error-correction data alone would streamline this process.
method: Fault-event probabilities are variational parameters optimized by gradient descent to minimize binary cross-entropy between tensor-network decoder predictions and experimental logical-observable outcomes, with analytical gradients from exact maximum-likelihood decoding.
result: On Google Sycamore circuit-level data, the learned noise models agree with independent reference error models to within ~1% logical error rate, and warm-started updates maintain near-optimal performance under synthetic noise drift.
conclusion: The principled, decoder-agnostic framework naturally extends to correlated noise, offering a practical path to continuously updated noise models for quantum error correction.

title: Encoding Compact U(1) Gauge Fields In Bosonic Modes With Gkp Stabilization
authors: Victor Ale, Tommaso Rainaldi, Enrique Rico, Felix Ringer, George Siopsis
abstract: ArXiv:2609.00167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compact lattice gauge theories are formulated in terms of angular variables and integer electric fluxes, while bosonic quantum hardware provides oscillator modes with continuous, unbounded quadratures. We bridge this gap with a one-to-one encoding. After Gauss's law is solved, each remaining gauge degree of freedom is carried by a single oscillator mode, with its interactions built from trigonometric gates, and a Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP)-type stabilizer provides the compactness that the hardware does not. The encoding becomes exact in the limit of infinite squeezing, and at finite squeezing, the leading imperfections act as small, computable shifts of physical observables rather than uncontrolled leakage. We apply the construction to compact QED[MATH] and derive the error budget at finite squeezing, characterizing the leading errors in closed form, and showing that they can be corrected, subtracted, or extrapolated away. We construct syndrome-extraction protocols that detect and remove the displacement component of photon loss, delimit the noise it does not reach, compare two choices of dynamical variables, and collect the scaling of mode count, gate count, and measurement cost. A one-plaquette example reproduces the exact compact-rotor dynamics, and real-time spectroscopy with controlled extrapolations recovers the exponentially small energy splitting between charge sectors, the seed of the monopole physics of the theory, at the percent level against its exact value.
tldr: This paper presents a novel encoding of compact U(1) lattice gauge fields into bosonic modes with GKP stabilization, enabling quantum simulation of gauge theories on continuous-variable hardware.
motivation: To simulate compact lattice gauge theories, which use angular variables and integer fluxes, on bosonic quantum hardware that naturally supports continuous variables, bridging the gap between the two formalisms.
method: They solve Gauss's law to reduce degrees of freedom, encode each remaining gauge degree of freedom in a single oscillator mode, use trigonometric gates for interactions, and introduce a GKP-type stabilizer to enforce compactness. They analyze finite-squeezing errors and design syndrome-extraction protocols to correct displacement errors from photon loss.
result: The encoding is exact at infinite squeezing, and at finite squeezing leading errors are small and correctable. They demonstrate the scheme on a one-plaquette example, reproducing exact compact-rotor dynamics and recovering the exponentially small energy splitting between charge sectors with percent-level accuracy.
conclusion: The work provides a practical and error-correctable approach to simulating compact gauge theories on continuous-variable quantum devices, offering a pathway to study gauge theory dynamics including monopole physics.

title: High-Rank Encoding Can Improve Approximate Quantum Error Correction
authors: Liang Jiang Bikun Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.00778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional quantum-code constructions encode pure logical states as pure code states, but this restriction can sacrifice performance. We show that intrinsic encoding randomness can improve optimal entanglement fidelity. We bound the loss from imposing a rank-one encoder and prove it is at most quadratic near perfect recovery after joint optimization. The optimized advantage survives small noise perturbations. An explicit noise family requires higher-rank encoders arbitrarily close to perfect recovery, with every optimal encoder mapping pure inputs to mixed code states.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that using higher-rank (mixed-state) encoders can improve the optimal entanglement fidelity of approximate quantum error correction, and provides bounds on the loss when restricting to standard rank-one encoders.
motivation: Conventional quantum error correction encodes pure logical states into pure code states, but this may compromise performance; the authors investigate whether allowing intrinsic encoding randomness (higher-rank encoders) can yield better approximate quantum error correction.
method: They analyze the optimal entanglement fidelity under joint optimization, bound the performance loss when the encoder is constrained to be rank-one (pure-state encoder), and construct an explicit noise family where higher-rank encoders are necessary to approach perfect recovery.
result: The loss from imposing a rank-one encoder is shown to be at most quadratic near perfect recovery, and there exist noise families for which every optimal encoder must map pure inputs to mixed code states, indicating that higher-rank encoding can be arbitrarily beneficial.
conclusion: Allowing quantum encoders to output mixed states can improve approximate quantum error correction performance, especially in the near-perfect recovery regime, and this advantage is robust to small noise.

title: Towards Unsupervised Representation Learning For Quantum Data: Quantum Models With Inference And Generation
authors: Robin Lorenz, Eric Brunner, Marcello Benedetti
abstract: ArXiv:2609.00372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With quantum sensors, simulators and networks emerging, a future of quantum technology may produce quantum states as data---that is, coherently rather than as classical measurement records---thus motivating the study of suitable quantum generalisations of modern machine learning, including the automated, unsupervised extraction of useful representations. Two ingredients are central to the latter: inference, mapping observations to latent representations, and generation, mapping latent states back to synthetic data. Both are related to each other and to joint distributions for training models by the chain-rule of classical probability theory. The fact that quantum states however lack such universal, standard factorisation property thus poses a challenge. Here we develop a conceptual and mathematical framework for unsupervised representation learning from quantum data. Models are joint quantum states over visible and latent systems; state-over-time maps provide a notion of factorisation into a marginal state and inference (generation) channel; models with inference (generation) are ambiguous states---states for which such factorisation obtains---subject to a further consistency condition on extended inference maps as data extension. These stipulations are restrictive: we show that non-trivial models must feature non-linear such maps to the extended space. For three representative state-over-time maps, we completely characterise the ambiguous states, uncovering a hierarchy tied to the positive-partial-transpose (PPT) criterion from entanglement theory. Notably, the Leifer-Spekkens construction supports inference and generation exactly for model classes of PPT states, thus allowing genuinely quantum visible-latent correlations. We also formulate quantum counterparts of exact and approximate inference training, explore weaker notions of data extension and sketch a future research programme.

title: Imaginarity Witnessing Enhancement Via Spectral Norms Of Witnesses
authors: Yuhang Xie, Yanjun Chu, Yushan Ding, Shao-Ming Fei
abstract: ArXiv:2609.00534v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum imaginarity is an essential physical resource that underpins key functionalities of modern quantum technologies. We improve imaginarity witnessing via the prior knowledge of imaginarity-witness operators. To this end, we derive a rigorous upper bound on the maximum expectation value of an imaginarity witness operator over the set of all free (real) quantum states, which is given by the spectral norm of the real component of the corresponding witness operator. For these four witness classes, we perform a comprehensive analysis of their completeness and finite completeness, the joint detection of shared imaginary quantum states by different witnesses, and the conditions for distinct witnesses to identify identical imaginary states. Our results advance the fundamental understanding of imaginarity detection and offer useful insights for both theoretical studies and experimental implementations of quantum imaginarity.

title: Nonlinear Fluctuating Hydrodynamics From Interacting Noisy Quantum Matter
authors: Alexios Christopoulos, Jo\~ao Costa, Stefano Scopa, Jacopo de Nardis, Zala Lenar\v{c}i\v{c}, Denis Bernard, Tony Jin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.00159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A universal characterization of non-equilibrium steady states in interacting quantum many-body systems remains one of the central challenges of statistical physics. Here, we address this problem for a paradigmatic model of diffusive interacting quantum matter---the boundary-driven XXZ spin chain with bulk dephasing---and derive, directly from its microscopic Lindblad dynamics, an emergent classical Macroscopic Fluctuation Theory (MFT) governing its large-scale fluctuations. title: Structure-Aware Placement And Routing Of Multi-Controlled Toffoli On Bivariate Bicycle Code Architectures
authors: Anik Basu Bhaumik, Suman Dutta, Siyi Wang, Anupam Chattopadhyay
abstract: ArXiv:2609.00852v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The multi-controlled Toffoli (MCT) gate is a fundamental primitive in quantum circuit design, with applications in quantum arithmetic, cryptanalysis, and algorithmic implementations. Being a high-level logical operation, the efficient decomposition of MCT gates into lower-level netlists has remained a major optimization challenge for decades. While emerging quantum error-correcting codes such as bivariate bicycle (BB) codes drastically reduce fault-tolerance overhead, realizing non-Clifford circuits on modular BB-code architectures introduces complex compilation bottlenecks governed by inter-module routing, factory density, and layout. Consequently, the mapping of MCT gates onto BB-code architectures remains relatively unexplored. In this paper, we overcome these challenges by mapping optimal-Toffoli-depth MCT decompositions (Dutta et al., PRA, 2025) onto BB-code-based fault-tolerant architectures via direct [MATH] state injection from an external magic state factory. We introduce a targeted placement strategy that exploits the binary-tree structure of MCT decompositions to co-locate interacting subtrees. This approach reduces inter-module instruction counts by up to [MATH] compared to a naive sequential first-fit placement. We also evaluate the impact of factory placement across different topologies, demonstrating that grid-based layouts yield up to a [MATH] reduction in inter-module instructions relative to linear architectures (Yoder et al., arXiv, 2025). Finally, we validate the practical viability of our compiled circuits by analyzing aggregate execution errors and logical failure probabilities using the bicycle-ISA error estimator bicycle_numerics provided by the Qiskit community, [URL].

They introduce a targeted placement strategy that exploits the binary-tree structure of the MCT decompositions to co-locate interacting subtrees, reducing inter-module instruction counts by up to 16.02% compared to a naive sequential first-fit placement. The paper also evaluates the impact of factory placement across different topologies, showing that grid-based layouts yield up to a 23.7% reduction in inter-module instructions relative to linear architectures. Finally, they validate practical viability by analyzing aggregate execution errors and logical failure probabilities using the bicycle-ISA error estimator bicycle_numerics from the Qiskit community.
